baaz.title: The Power of Quantifier Shifts
abstract: Quantifier shifts are one of the oldest proof methods, but they are orthogonal to the cut free format: They can shorten proofs non-elementarily. (The proof is based on the sequence of proofs exhibiting a non-elementary difference between proofs with cuts and cut-free proofs by Orevkov). The cost is, however, that those proofs are globally sound but locally unsound. (Their subderivations might be unsound in contrast to the Hilbert concept of proof). In non-classical logics these calculi are only sound when all quantifier shifts are added. This characterizes all intermediate logics where Skolemization and the epsilon calculus is conservative (in contrast to the epsilon theorem which holds only for finite-valued Gödel logics).

pinsker.title: The Power of Polymorphisms: The Triangle of Universal Algebra, Model Theory, and Theoretical Computer Science
abstract: I am going to survey tight connections between universal algebra, model theory, and theoretical computer science (specifically, constraint satisfaction) established in the past 25 years, and try to provide the audience with an intuition for them. At the center of this tutorial will be the notion of a polymorphism.

A polymorphism of a relational structure A is a multivariate function on the structure leaving all relations of A invariant. It is a generalization of an endomorphism, which is a unary function under which A is invariant, or of an automorphism, which is a unary function under which A is (strongly) invariant.

Similarly to the automorphism group or the endomorphism monoid of A, the set of all polymorphisms of A, called the polymorphism clone Pol(A) of A, provides us with structural information about A, in particular which other structures A can define, interpret, or construct (in a certain precise way). Since the polymorphism clone Pol(A) consists of multivariate functions on the same domain A, it can be viewed as an algebra, just like the set of automorphisms can be viewed as a group. Therefore, algebraic methods can be used to investigate the polymorphism clone Pol(A), and hence derive information about the original structure A. This is the link between model theory and universal algebra.

Every relational structure A defines a computational problem, the Constraint Satisfaction Problem CSP(A), where given a list of variables and atomic statements (called constraints) about these variables in the language of A one has to find a solution, i.e., a map from the variables into A such that all atomic statements are satisfied. This kind of computational problem is extremely general: every computational problem is polynomial-time (Turing) equivalent to CSP(A) for a suitable structure A. Since the polymorphisms of A leave the set of solutions of any instance of CSP(A) invariant, they are central in the study of the computational complexity of CSP(A): in fact, the computational complexity of CSP(A), certain model-theoretic properties of A, and the algebraic structure of the polymorphism clone Pol(A) are tightly connected, with nontrivial implications holding in all directions of this triangle.

kuznetsov.title: Infinitary Substructural Logics
abstract: Substructural logics are logical systems lacking certain principles called structural rules: contraction, weakening, commutativity. Such logics find their applications in linguistics (Lambek grammars), computer science (reasoning about programs), and other areas. They are also interesting from a purely mathematical point of view. In these lectures, we shall discuss extensions of substructural logics by infinitary proof-theoretic mechanisms. Those naturally arise when the logics in question are extended with fixed point operators, a typical example of which is the Kleene star. We shall discuss infinitary proof theory and algorithmic complexity results for such systems.

gabelaia.title: Introduction to Semantics of Modal Logic
abstract: In this course we will provide an introduction to the semantical treatment of modal logic. First two lectures will be devoted to introducing basic modal language, Hilbert-style axiomatic definition of normal modal logics and their Kripke semantics. The two remaining lectures will address topological semantics, including the diamond-as-closure interpretation, diamond-as-derivative interpretation and polyhedral semantics.

baratashvili.title: The Georgian Language: Exploring Its Phonological and Morphosyntactic Peculiarities
abstract: Georgian, a Kartvelian language, provides particularly rich material for formal and typological study of morphosyntax. Its morphological system combines relatively transparent affixal sequences with substantial fusion and morphophonological interaction, making it difficult to classify as exclusively agglutinative or fusional. This lecture examines three central areas of Georgian grammar: word-internal morphological structure, polypersonal agreement and valency, and screeve-dependent patterns of case marking and alignment.

The first part considers the relationship between Georgian phonotactics and morphological structure. Georgian permits complex consonant clusters, including harmonic clusters and longer sequences such as those found in gvprtskvnis ‘(s)he peels us’, gvbrdɣvnis ‘(s)he plucks us’, and so on. The maximal number of consonants at the edge of morphemes in a compound word is 11 in the artificially created but fully grammatical word vepxvtmbrdɣvneli ‘(the person) who plucks the tiger/panther’. Such forms raise important questions concerning syllabification, morpheme boundaries, and the interaction between phonological and morphological organisation.

The second part addresses Georgian polypersonal (namely, bipersonal) agreement and argument structure. Depending on the verb and construction, a finite verb may index more than one core participant, including the subject, direct object, and indirect object. Particular attention will be paid to the distribution of the v-set and m-set person markers and to the interaction between person, number, grammatical relation, and argument hierarchy. The lecture will also examine valency-changing and voice-related morphology, including causative formation, dynamic and stative passives, and the system traditionally described in terms of subjective, objective, locative, and neutral version (the typologically valid term is applicative). Restrictions on agreement and competition between person markers will be evaluated as evidence for the hierarchical organisation of the Georgian verbal complex.

The final part examines the interaction between tense, aspect, mood, verb class, case marking, and agreement. Georgian displays distinct alignment patterns across its three screeve series. In Series I, the agent of a transitive verb is typically in the nominative and the patient in the dative; in Series II, the agent of a transitive verb is in the ergative and the patient in the nominative; and in Series III, many transitive constructions display an inversion pattern in which the agent is in the dative and the patient in the nominative. A related pattern also occurs with many experiencer and affective predicates. These alternations interact with the traditional four-class classification of Georgian verbs: Class I transitive verbs, Class II intransitive and passive verbs, Class III active intransitive verbs, and Class IV indirect or experiencer verbs. The lecture will consider whether Georgian split ergativity is primarily a matter of morphological case marking or whether it also has syntactic consequences.

The theoretical discussion will be accompanied by interactive exercises based on glossed Georgian data. Students will analyse the internal structure of complex verb forms, identify agreement markers and their controllers, and predict changes in case marking and agreement when clauses are transformed from one screeve series to another.
